slides.title: Rumbles travel through both air and ground
body: Elephant **rumbles** are low-frequency vocalizations with energy that can propagate as airborne pressure changes and as ground motion. Limberger and colleagues recorded African savanna elephants with a co-located infrasound sensor and three-component seismometer during a month of zoo monitoring.

A **spectrogram** represents frequency content over time. Corresponding rumbles appeared in both recording channels, commonly with fundamentals around 10–25 Hz and harmonics above 25 Hz. Individual rumble events lasted approximately 1–8 s in this dataset.

Footfalls produced strong seismic transients without equivalent infrasonic events. Matching the channels therefore distinguished vocal activity from locomotion more reliably than either channel alone; recordable ground energy does not establish how far elephants can perceive it.

slides.title: Brain mass differs across species and sex
body: Shah and colleagues compared postmortem brains from Asian elephants, _Elephas maximus_, and African savanna elephants, _Loxodonta africana_. They combined documented specimens with earlier brain-weight records, retaining species, sex and age information rather than treating all elephants as one anatomical category.

Adult female Asian brains averaged 5,346 g, compared with 4,417 g in African females. African male brains averaged 5,603 g. The Asian female brains were larger despite the species having a smaller average female body mass.

Newborn brains averaged 1,806 g across the two species, approximately one-third of the pooled adult value. The substantial postnatal increase describes anatomical development; neither brain mass nor these cross-sectional comparisons measure learning capacity, auditory performance or intelligence directly.

slides.title: MRI separates cortical gray and white matter
body: **Magnetic resonance imaging**, or MRI, distinguishes tissues through their physical responses to magnetic fields and radiofrequency stimulation. Shah and colleagues acquired T1- and T2-weighted scans of postmortem elephant brains and segmented the outer cortical surface and the gray–white matter boundary.

**Gray matter** contains neuronal cell bodies and local processes; **white matter** is dominated by axons and their myelin sheaths. Comparing both MRI contrasts helped the investigators recognize boundaries despite artifacts and reconstruct cortical tissue volumes.

Asian elephants had a larger cortical gray-matter proportion than African savanna elephants in the available specimens. Segmentation measures tissue geometry, not synaptic connectivity or regional neural activity. The comparison therefore establishes a species difference in brain organization without assigning that difference to a particular sensory computation.

slides.title: Brain size does not specify cortical neuron number
body: Herculano-Houzel and colleagues partitioned a fixed African elephant hemisphere into anatomically identified regions and used the **isotropic fractionator**, a tissue-processing method that estimates cell numbers from suspended nuclei. Whole-brain estimates doubled the counts from the analyzed hemisphere.

The cerebral cortex contained approximately 5.6 billion neurons, while the complete brain estimate was about 257 billion. A large cortex can contain fewer neurons per unit tissue than a smaller cortex; neuron number and tissue mass are therefore distinct anatomical measurements.

The elephant cortical estimate followed the scaling relationship of other afrotherian mammals rather than the primate relationship. The preparation supplied detailed regional counts but destroyed local tissue architecture during counting, so it did not identify functional auditory circuits, synapses or individual neuronal response properties.

slides.title: Most counted neurons reside in the cerebellum
body: The **cerebellum** is a hindbrain structure associated with movement coordination and sensory–motor processing. Regional cell counting in the African elephant yielded approximately 250.7 billion cerebellar neurons, about 97.5% of the estimated total brain neurons.

The ratio was roughly 45 cerebellar neurons for every cortical neuron, substantially above the approximately four-to-one relationship described for many other sampled mammals. Thus, the exceptionally high elephant whole-brain count largely reflects cerebellar organization rather than a corresponding excess of cortical neurons.

The authors proposed contributions from trunk control and other sensory specializations, including low-frequency communication. These are functional hypotheses derived from anatomical scaling. The count did not test cerebellar activity during trunk contact, rumble perception or seismic-playback responses.

slides.title: Cerebellar proportion also varies between species
body: Shah and colleagues delineated the cerebellum in MRI volumes and compared cerebellar size with total brain size. The method separated an absolute tissue measurement from a **relative proportion**, the fraction of the complete brain occupied by that region.

Asian elephant cerebella averaged 19.1% of brain weight, whereas African savanna cerebella averaged 22.3%. The species differed in proportional allocation even though the available absolute cerebellar weights were comparable.

The finding complements regional neuron counts: a large cerebellar fraction and a high cerebellar neuron count describe related but different features. MRI does not identify cell populations, and proportional anatomy does not prove superior motor control or seismic sensitivity. Comparisons also remain limited by preservation differences and the available species, sex and age distribution.

slides.title: The ventral brainstem contains a trunk candidate
body: Reveyaz and colleagues studied fixed elephant brainstems to identify a candidate central representation of trunk touch. The **trigeminal system**, associated with cranial nerve V, conveys somatic sensation from the face and trunk rather than motor commands to trunk muscles.

Paired protrusions approximately 1 cm behind the pons contained intensely cytochrome-oxidase-reactive tissue. **Cytochrome oxidase** is a mitochondrial enzyme whose histochemical activity indicates local energy metabolism; the proposed trunk module was also densely vascularized.

Earlier anatomical descriptions called these protrusions the inferior olive. The new study proposed a trigeminal identity using several converging anatomical tests. This assignment remains explicitly putative: staining can locate a specialized tissue compartment, but it does not record touch-evoked responses or establish its receptive fields.

slides.title: Fiber anatomy distinguishes olive from trigeminal tissue
body: The **inferior olive** supplies climbing fibers to the cerebellum in mammals. Reveyaz and colleagues used antibodies against **peripherin**, a neuronal structural protein, to delineate the elephant olivo-cerebellar pathway and test whether the prominent ventral bumps belonged to it.

The labeled pathway connected the cerebellum with a separate dorsolateral nucleus that had a folded cellular architecture characteristic of an olive. It did not provide the expected climbing-fiber connection to the ventral protrusions assigned as trigeminal tissue.

This anatomical control supports separating a candidate trunk sensory representation from an olivo-cerebellar structure. The argument depends on pathway labeling and comparative morphology, not on the bump’s external position alone. It still does not establish which tactile stimuli activate individual neurons or how their activity reaches higher sensory centers.

slides.title: Trigeminal modules repeat along the brainstem
body: Serial sections permitted Reveyaz and colleagues to compare candidate trunk modules along the anterior–posterior axis of the brainstem. A **nucleus** is a centrally located group of neurons; repeated nuclei can process related peripheral inputs at different anatomical levels.

The proposed **principal trigeminal nucleus**, abbreviated Pr5, was the most anterior and largest trunk representation. Smaller posterior modules were assigned to the spinal trigeminal subdivisions pars oralis, pars interpolaris and pars caudalis using comparative organization and tissue boundaries.

Nissl staining, which labels cell-body-associated material, helped distinguish cellular regions from surrounding fiber tracts. The repeated architecture supports an organized brainstem sensory system. Individual module identities and peripheral assignments remain anatomical proposals, because invasive sensory mapping and pathway tracing were not available in living elephants.

slides.title: Trunk-module cells align with myelinated bundles
body: Golgi staining revealed neuronal processes within the candidate trigeminal trunk module. **Dendrites** are neuronal branches receiving inputs; **myelin** is an insulating sheath around many axons. The principal neuronal dendritic trees tended to elongate along the local axon-bundle orientation.

After alignment to the bundles, the measured dendritic trees were approximately twice as long along the bundle axis as across it. NeuN labeling identified neurons, while DAPI labeled DNA-containing nuclei, allowing neuronal and non-neuronal populations to be distinguished.

The broader tissue analysis estimated roughly 108 non-neuronal cells per neuron. This unusually sparse neuronal organization cautions against equating module volume with neuron abundance. Morphological categories and alignment do not reveal neurotransmitter identity, synaptic partners or the activity patterns used for tactile discrimination.

slides.title: Myelin stripes correspond to trunk folds
body: The candidate trunk module contained prominent stripes visible in fresh tissue and confirmed with fluorescent myelin staining. Reveyaz and colleagues compared the number, orientation and arrangement of those stripes with the folds of the same elephant’s trunk.

They counted 65 dorsally ending stripes alongside 64 dorsal trunk folds, with similar correspondences for other stripe and fold classes. The proposed map allocated much more neural distance to distal trunk regions: the reported trunk-to-neural length ratio changed from about 1,000:1 proximally to 5:1 at the finger.

**Sensory magnification** means disproportionate neural space devoted to a peripheral region. Here it is inferred from anatomical correspondence, not measured receptive fields. Section angle affected stripe visibility, and the authors proposed that some stripe axons separate fold-related domains rather than acting as ordinary local connections.

slides.title: Species-specific trunk use matches candidate maps
body: Asian elephants commonly wrap the trunk around objects, whereas African savanna elephants can pinch with two opposing tip fingers. Reveyaz and colleagues compared brainstem tissue organization with these differences in peripheral anatomy and object manipulation.

The candidate principal trunk module contained approximately 640,000 neurons in Asian elephants and 740,000 in African elephants. Asian modules had enlarged representations assigned to regions involved in wrapping, while finger-related regions differed with the species’ tip morphology.

The relationship is consistent with sensory specialization for different manipulative strategies. It remains a comparison of postmortem anatomy and observed morphology, rather than a causal manipulation of trunk use. The proposed peripheral assignments do not establish which neurons detect ground contact or whether these trigeminal modules mediate seismic communication.

slides.title: Facial nuclei provide a separate motor organization
body: Kaufmann and colleagues examined fixed brainstems and facial nerves to characterize elephant facial motor control. The **facial nucleus** contains cranial nerve VII motor neurons, anatomically distinct from the trigeminal sensory nuclei associated with trunk sensation.

Nissl-stained sections supported approximately 54,000 facial-nucleus neurons in Asian elephants and 63,000 in African elephants. The estimates were checked using different counting approaches and, where possible, against facial-nerve axon counts.

The nucleus contained unusually elongated dorsal and lateral subdivisions, proposed to innervate trunk muscles. The correspondence follows comparative motor organization, large neuron populations and matching peripheral anatomy. These fixed-tissue observations identify candidate motor representations without measuring muscle activation or proving the specific commands issued during trunk handling or listening postures.

Peripheral axon counts provide a separate anatomical check on central cell counts, although they do not identify each neuron’s target muscle.

slides.title: Larger African ears have larger motor allocations
body: The **auricularis branch** of the facial nerve supplies ear musculature. Kaufmann and colleagues compared ear size, this motor nerve branch and the medial facial subnucleus in Asian and African savanna elephants.

African elephants had larger ears, a thicker auricularis branch and more medial-subnucleus neurons. Reported mean counts were approximately 12,000 neurons in African elephants and 7,500 in Asian elephants. Nerve-axon counts and comparative mammalian anatomy supported assigning this region to ear motor control.

The agreement links an enlarged peripheral structure with increased central motor allocation. Ear positioning can influence how sound reaches the animal, but this anatomical study did not test sound-localization performance. It also did not show that these motor neurons close the ear canal or selectively enhance ground-vibration reception.

The agreement links an enlarged peripheral structure with increased central motor allocation. A proposed role for ear posture in hearing requires behavioral or mechanical evidence beyond the cell counts.

slides.title: Distal motor neurons are exceptionally large
body: Kaufmann and colleagues reconstructed neuron positions in dorsal and lateral facial subdivisions and measured cell-body size along their elongated axes. **Somata** are neuronal cell bodies; their size can vary independently of the number of neurons in a region.

Cells became larger toward the putative distal trunk representation, with some estimated volumes near 100,000 µm³. The corresponding gradients were much weaker or absent in the comparison mammalian facial nuclei analyzed in the study.

The authors proposed that these large cells support long axons and demanding control of distal trunk musculature. The interpretation is anatomically plausible but was not tested by conduction-velocity measurements, neuromuscular recordings or manipulations of individual motor units. Large somata alone do not establish faster sensory detection or more precise temporal coding.

slides.title: Trunk tips have candidate motor foveae
body: African elephant trunk tips have dorsal and ventral fingers used for pinching, while Asian elephant tips have a single dorsal finger and often wrap around objects. Kaufmann and colleagues related these peripheral differences to cell distributions in the facial motor nucleus.

**Motor fovea** denotes a proposed concentration of neural resources for a particularly dexterous effector. The dorsal subdivision contained concentrations of large neurons in both species, while the lateral subdivision had a marked distal concentration in African elephants.

The published anatomy is consistent with distinct finger-control demands. It does not identify individual finger muscles by direct stimulation, and the correspondence is not a measured map of task-related firing. Sensory magnification in the trigeminal system and motor specialization in the facial system are complementary hypotheses supported by different anatomical preparations.

slides.title: Feet combine load-bearing tissues and sensory structures
body: Bouley and colleagues examined preserved Asian elephant feet to locate structures that might detect ground vibration. The forefoot had a rounder external profile than the hindfoot, and both contained substantial supporting tissues between the skin and skeletal elements.

The researchers sampled sagittal slices through different digits, concentrating on tissue approximately 6 cm above the sole. A **digital cushion** is the specialized soft supporting tissue beneath the digits; its distal portion and the overlying dermis were analyzed separately.

The preparation linked microscopic receptor locations to the foot’s gross geometry rather than assuming uniform sensation across the sole. Preserved tissue establishes the location of candidate receptors, but its mechanical properties differ from a loaded living foot. Vibration transfer under different postures was therefore a hypothesis, not a direct measurement.

slides.title: Histological sampling localizes candidate receptors
body: Bouley and colleagues divided the distal foot tissue into proximal and distal rows, then processed it into paraffin sections stained with **hematoxylin and eosin**, or H&E. This stain differentiates cellular and connective-tissue components for light microscopy.

They identified Pacinian corpuscles by a central nerve process, concentric surrounding lamellae and a distinct outer capsule. Traced receptor profiles were overlaid on the original foot slice, preserving the relationship between microscopic observations and anterior, middle and posterior positions.

**Density** was expressed as corpuscle profiles per mm² of sectioned tissue. More profiles occurred in the distal than proximal row. These are section-based anatomical measurements, not a complete count of all living receptors or a measurement of their vibration thresholds. Tissue processing also produced shrinkage that affects absolute dimensions.

slides.title: Pacinian corpuscles surround a central neurite
body: A **Pacinian corpuscle** is an encapsulated mechanoreceptor composed of a nerve ending surrounded by concentric lamellae. A **mechanoreceptor** responds to mechanical deformation; the elephant foot sections contained recognizable central neurites, interlamellar spaces and an external connective-tissue capsule.

The published H&E micrograph includes a 0.1 mm scale bar, placing these structures at a tissue scale appropriate for local deformation. The central **neurite** is the neuronal process, while the surrounding lamellae are non-neuronal components of the receptor organ.

Pacinian morphology makes vibration sensing a credible candidate function. Nevertheless, the elephant study did not record receptor potentials or action potentials. It did not identify the molecular transduction channel, demonstrate a 20–40 Hz best frequency or determine whether these receptors are necessary for seismic-playback responses.

slides.title: Many foot corpuscles occur in clusters
body: Serial H&E sections permitted Bouley and colleagues to follow corpuscles through adjacent tissue planes rather than interpreting each profile in isolation. Individual organs appeared, changed outline and disappeared as the cutting plane passed through a cluster.

Approximately 80% of the observed corpuscles occurred in clusters, commonly containing three or four organs and occasionally as many as 18. A reconstructed serial sequence spanned 400 µm of tissue, preserving the changing relation between adjacent encapsulated structures.

Clustering concentrates candidate mechanoreceptive elements in localized tissue compartments. It does not establish that those receptors share an axon, converge on one central neuron or have identical frequency tuning. The study’s serial anatomy helps distinguish neighboring organs from repeated intersections of a single irregularly shaped structure.

slides.title: Three-dimensional anatomy resolves receptor boundaries
body: Bouley and colleagues reconstructed an encapsulated receptor cluster from traced serial histological sections. The original article’s three-dimensional rendering retained separate contours for individual Pacinian corpuscles, allowing structures that overlapped in a single section to be distinguished.

The reconstruction revealed complex shape changes and branching profiles rather than a set of identical spherical organs. Complete structures could be followed from their first appearance to their disappearance, whereas incompletely sampled structures could not supply reliable total volumes.

This method clarifies organ geometry and the limitations of two-dimensional profile counts. The published reconstruction is an anatomical result, not a simulation of receptor activity. It contains no measured ground-to-nerve transfer function, so the arrangement cannot yet be converted into a demonstrated seismic detection threshold or a proven neural coding scheme.

slides.title: Receptor distribution supports a posture hypothesis
body: Bouley and colleagues found corpuscle distributions concentrated near the anterior and posterior foot regions. The traced profiles placed about 52% of forefoot corpuscles anteriorly and 47% of hindfoot corpuscles posteriorly, rather than distributing them evenly through the sampled tissue.

The authors related this anatomy to leaning and weight-shifting postures observed during seismic-playback responses. Greater contact or loading at receptor-rich regions might improve transfer of substrate vibration to the receptor organs.

This **coupling hypothesis** links a possible change in mechanical input to a possible change in sensation. Neither local pressure nor receptor firing was recorded during the postures. Freezing might also reduce self-generated movement noise, and bone conduction remains an alternative route. Behavioral posture alone cannot isolate the mechanism of ground-signal detection.

slides.title: An operant task measures auditory detection
body: Heffner and Heffner measured hearing in a young Asian elephant using an **operant task**, in which an animal learns a response through its consequences. The elephant pressed a central button to initiate a trial, then selected a response associated with the presented sound.

Fruit-flavored sugar solution reinforced correct choices. Loudspeakers and response buttons permitted controlled tests of sound detection, frequency discrimination and left–right localization within the same preparation. Sound pressure was calibrated rather than inferred from the speaker setting.

The procedure converts an animal’s report into a repeatable psychophysical measurement. Training, motivation, ambient noise and response rules can influence observed thresholds, so the results describe behavioral performance under the tested conditions. A threshold is not a direct measurement of cochlear hair-cell sensitivity or a species-wide constant.

slides.title: The audiogram extends into infrasound
body: An **audiogram** plots the sound level needed for detection against frequency. Heffner and Heffner obtained similar curves with the speaker directed toward the left and right ears, checking for gross asymmetry and sound-field problems.

The elephant detected 16 Hz at 65 dB sound-pressure level; the low-frequency limit at 60 dB was estimated as 17 Hz. Best measured sensitivity occurred around 1 kHz at 8 dB. The 60 dB high-frequency limit was approximately 10.5 kHz.

**Sound-pressure level**, or SPL, expresses acoustic pressure relative to a standard reference, here 20 µPa. Background noise lay near thresholds over part of the intermediate-frequency range, so the animal’s true sensitivity there may have been better than the measured curve. An audible frequency range does not establish the detection range of distant natural calls.

slides.title: Frequency discrimination is strongest at low frequencies
body: Heffner and Heffner presented alternating tones and rewarded choices based on whether their frequencies differed. A **frequency difference limen** is the smallest discriminable frequency change under a specified behavioral criterion, rather than the lowest frequency an animal can hear.

At 250 and 500 Hz, the elephant detected fractional changes around 0.005 under the 75%-correct criterion. Discrimination became poorer around 1 kHz and declined further at higher test frequencies. The tones were presented well above detection threshold, with level variation reducing simple loudness cues.

This separation of detection from discrimination matters for communication: hearing a rumble does not guarantee that all frequency contours can be resolved. The study measured differences between controlled tones, not recognition of individual elephants, alarm meaning or discrimination of complete naturally propagated seismic calls.

slides.title: Brief broadband sounds can be localized precisely
body: Heffner and Heffner tested left–right localization with single clicks and 100 ms bursts of broadband noise. **Azimuth** is horizontal direction; varying the angular separation between the speakers measured how well the elephant distinguished nearby source positions.

The animal localized widely separated sources accurately, with broadband thresholds around 1°. Fast-onset noise with a 0.1 ms rise time supported better small-angle performance than noise with a 50 ms rise time or a single click.

Brief sounds reduced opportunities for head scanning or tracking a continuing source. The result therefore supports precise localization from available auditory cues rather than movement toward a sustained sound. It does not identify the responsible brainstem neurons, nor does a broadband threshold predict equally accurate localization of low-frequency tonal rumbles or ground vibrations.

slides.title: Tone localization depends on frequency
body: Heffner and Heffner tested brief pure tones from 125 Hz to 8 kHz at different source separations. Presenting audible stimuli well above threshold helped separate difficulty locating a sound from failure to detect its presence.

Localization was strongest at 125 and 250 Hz, intermediate at 500 Hz through 2 kHz, and poor at 4 and 8 kHz. Even at large separations, tonal performance was less complete than the nearly perfect performance obtained with broadband sounds.

The frequency dependence is consistent with different **binaural cues**, information derived by comparing inputs to the two ears. Low-frequency timing and phase differences can support direction judgments, while higher-frequency intensity differences may contribute. slides.title: Phase ambiguity limits a timing-only account
body: An **interaural time difference** is the difference in arrival time between the two ears. For a repeating tone, the corresponding **phase difference** specifies the relative position within its oscillation cycle; phase becomes ambiguous when different delays correspond to the same repeating pattern.

Heffner and Heffner tested tones at 60° separation and 40 dB above detection threshold. Performance remained relatively good around 500 Hz through 2 kHz, beyond the range where a simple unambiguous phase comparison was expected to suffice for the elephant’s large head.

The authors therefore proposed contributions from interaural intensity differences in addition to timing. This inference explains why one cue cannot account for the full behavioral function. It is a psychophysical constraint, not a direct recording of coincidence detectors, phase-locking neurons or excitatory–inhibitory comparisons in the elephant brainstem.

slides.title: High-frequency noise outperforms high-frequency tones
body: Heffner and Heffner replaced pure tones with filtered noise bands to test whether poor high-frequency localization reflected a general inability to use high-frequency sound. **Narrow-band noise** contains a restricted range of frequencies while retaining temporal and spectral variation.

The elephant localized bands centered at 4 and 8 kHz substantially better than corresponding pure tones. The filtered bands were localized with accuracy comparable to broadband noise; additional testing of high-pass noise above 8 kHz yielded a threshold around 0.7°.

Additional temporal or spectral information can support a direction judgment when a single tone is insufficient. The elephant localized bands centered at 4 and 8 kHz substantially better than corresponding pure tones. The filtered bands were localized with accuracy comparable to broadband noise; additional testing of high-pass noise above 8 kHz yielded a threshold around 0.7°.

slides.title: Bone conduction can move ossicles relative to the skull
body: **Bone conduction** is transmission to the inner ear through vibration of skull tissues rather than solely through airborne pressure at the eardrum. O’Connell-Rodwell and colleagues mechanically stimulated cadaveric elephant and human temporal bones and measured motion with three-dimensional laser Doppler vibrometry.

The **ossicles** are the malleus, incus and stapes of the middle ear. Measurements at the umbo, stapes and cochlear promontory distinguished ossicular movement from movement of the surrounding bony reference over 12–11,000 Hz.

Relative stapes motion can contribute to cochlear stimulation when skull vibration and ossicular inertia differ. The preparation directly measured mechanics, but it lacked living neural responses, an intact weight-bearing body and behavioral detection. It therefore supports one component of a candidate seismic-hearing route without proving transmission from the feet to auditory perception.

slides.title: Differential velocity separates local from shared motion
body: O’Connell-Rodwell and colleagues projected three-dimensional velocities along the stapes piston direction, the direction relevant to its motion into and out of the inner-ear entrance. Comparing ossicular velocity with promontory velocity reduced the influence of motion shared by the entire specimen.

**Differential velocity** describes that relative motion normalized to the bony reference. Both magnitude and phase were measured, because a large displacement of the specimen does not necessarily imply substantial motion between the ossicles and cochlear capsule.

The normalized response changed systematically with frequency and differed between measurement sites. The study screened specimens for visible middle-ear pathology and maintained controlled mechanical stimulation. Cadaver preservation, open surgical access and varied elephant ages limit extension to intact hearing, particularly when estimating a perceptual threshold from a mechanical transfer measurement.

slides.title: Elephant bone-conduction resonance is lower
body: A **resonance** is a frequency range where the mechanical system has a characteristic enhanced response. O’Connell-Rodwell and colleagues compared normalized ossicular motion in elephant and human temporal-bone preparations under bone-conduction stimulation.

The measured bone-conduction resonance was approximately 400 Hz in elephants and 1,200 Hz in humans. Below the respective resonances, elephant stapes differential-velocity magnitudes were around three to four times greater than human values.

The authors linked the lower resonance to elephant middle-ear mass and its distribution. This provides direct comparative mechanical evidence consistent with low-frequency specialization. It does not mean that elephants perceive a sound as three to four times louder, and it does not establish a corresponding multiple in communication distance; perception also depends on cochlear and neural processing and environmental transmission.

slides.title: Low-frequency motion plateaus below about 200 Hz
body: The bone-conduction study followed relative ossicular motion into frequencies below the main resonance. Above approximately 200 Hz but below resonance, the differential-velocity magnitude decreased at roughly 12 dB per octave as stimulus frequency fell.

Below approximately 200 Hz, the measured stapes response plateaued in both elephant and human preparations rather than continuing that decline. Phase measurements supplied complementary information about the timing of the mechanical response in this low-frequency region.

The finding favors better low-frequency mechanical transmission than a simple continuation of the higher-frequency trend would predict. The authors also proposed enhancement through elephant ear-canal occlusion. That muscle-dependent mechanism was not demonstrated in living animals here, and neither the plateau nor the proposal identifies the sensory route actually used during ground-borne alarm responses.

slides.title: A buried source isolates ground-borne stimulation
body: O’Connell-Rodwell and colleagues played seismic replicas of alarm calls to wild African elephant breeding herds at Mushara waterhole in Etosha National Park. Buried mechanical shakers delivered the signal to the ground, approximately 30 m from the waterhole.

A **geophone** measures ground motion, while a microphone measures airborne pressure. Near and remote sensors monitored the two media, permitting the investigators to check whether a response attributed to ground vibration could instead be caused by sound radiated into the air.

The trial included a 5 min observation period and a 3 min playback phase containing repeated 15 s signals. Observers recorded spacing, vigilance and time at the waterhole. This field preparation tested the sufficiency of ground-delivered information for a response, rather than requiring the researchers to assume an anatomical detection route.

slides.title: Microphone controls check airborne leakage
body: In the seismic-playback study, stimulation strength had to balance ground detectability against unintended airborne radiation. High-level calibration signals could couple to the air, so the behavioral trials used a lower level with concurrent microphone monitoring.

Near-source geophones recorded increased energy in the 40–60 Hz region during playback, while the microphones did not detect a corresponding signal in that frequency band. The investigators also used signal-matching analyses to assess possible airborne contamination.

This control narrows the interpretation to a response elicited by ground-delivered stimulation under the tested conditions. Estimated levels at elephant positions depended on attenuation and background activity, so they were not direct measurements at every foot. The study established neither an absolute seismic threshold nor a maximum communication range across different soils.

slides.title: Seismic alarm playback changes herd behavior
body: Seismic alarm-call playback caused elephant breeding herds to form tighter groups and leave the waterhole sooner than comparison herds without the stimulus. The experiment measured these behavioral endpoints separately from individual scanning or freezing events.

Orientation also became nonrandom after playback, with many elephants facing approximately perpendicular to the source direction. Vigilant behaviors increased, but that change was less securely established than the changes in spacing and waterhole duration.

The response is consistent with detecting biologically relevant ground-borne information and organizing a defensive group response. It does not prove that recipients decoded a particular alarm meaning, and orientation is not a measured localization threshold. The approximately 30 m delivery geometry also cannot establish proposed kilometer-scale natural seismic communication distances.

slides.title: Call comparisons test more than vibration detection
body: O’Connell-Rodwell and colleagues compared seismic alarm rumbles recorded from the local Etosha population with unfamiliar alarm rumbles from Amboseli. Controls included no stimulation and artificial warble tones with broadly comparable low-frequency content and duration.

Alarm stimuli were bandpass filtered from 10 Hz to approximately 50–60 Hz, retaining the fundamental and second harmonic. The warble control varied around 30 Hz by 3 Hz at a 1 Hz modulation rate during 3 s tones.

These contrasts ask whether all low-frequency ground stimulation produces the same response. Randomized trial order and behavior scoring without knowledge of trial type reduced predictable observation effects. Call category, caller familiarity and detailed frequency modulation were not independently matched, so a response difference cannot be attributed uniquely to recognition of a familiar individual.

slides.title: Signal matching confirms a ground stimulus
body: The familiar-call experiment monitored a microphone and geophone during each seismic playback. A **matched filter** compares a recording with the known stimulus pattern, allowing a weak copy of the stimulus to be distinguished from unrelated background noise.

The stimulus-aligned peak appeared in the geophone record without a corresponding microphone peak above the study’s contamination criterion. Trials with evidence of sufficient airborne coupling were excluded before the behavioral comparison.

The paired measurements strengthen the case that observed responses were triggered by a ground-delivered signal rather than its ordinary airborne counterpart. They do not eliminate every possible unrecorded acoustic signal at each animal’s ears, and they do not distinguish foot mechanoreception from bone-conducted input. slides.title: Familiar alarms elicit stronger defensive responses
body: The familiar alarm-call treatment produced increased vigilance and reduced herd spacing after playback. Published spacing estimates changed from approximately 0.91 to 0.36 body lengths, linking a ground-delivered signal to a coordinated tightening of the group.

The joint behavioral change was established for familiar calls, whereas the control and unfamiliar-call treatments did not produce an equally secure overall effect. That comparison supports differential responses to different biological seismic signals, rather than indiscriminate reaction to any ground vibration.

The outcome does not establish a neural representation of caller identity. Familiar calls also differed in their frequency modulation, and the experiments did not independently manipulate familiarity and urgency. The behavior is therefore consistent with recognition or graded threat assessment, while the basis of the discrimination remains unresolved.

slides.title: Frequency contours leave recognition unresolved
body: The alarm-call investigators extracted frequency contours to compare the structures of familiar, unfamiliar and control stimuli. A **frequency contour** describes how a call’s dominant frequency changes over its duration, rather than only reporting its average frequency.

The treatments were recorded elephant-generated vibration, artificial white noise and their combination. Each 6 min track contained 2 min of silence, 2 min of treatment and 2 min of silence, separating baseline, stimulation and subsequent behavior.

Recorded ground and airborne channels checked the delivered stimulus. Repeated elephant segments and noise controls tested whether vibration type affected the response rather than vibration presence alone. body: Mortimer and colleagues observed movement away from the trial location during treatments containing human-generated seismic noise. The combined elephant-plus-noise treatment produced a particularly strong retreat pattern, while elephant-only vibrations produced less movement away.

The treatment differences support detection and discrimination of ground-borne noise with behavioral consequences consistent with risk avoidance. slides.title: Freezing and scanning accompany noise responses
body: The seismic-noise experiments separately measured head scanning and freezing, which are behavior categories rather than direct recordings of sensory processing. **Freezing** denotes a temporary cessation of movement; scanning involves changes in head orientation.

Treatments containing human-generated noise increased these behaviors during the playback period compared with relevant silent periods. The joint changes in movement, scanning and freezing provide a richer description of the response than retreat alone.

Freezing could reduce self-generated ground noise, while scanning could alter available directional information. Those proposed functions were not isolated experimentally. transcript: The seismic-noise experiments separately measured head scanning and freezing, which are behavior categories rather than direct recordings of sensory processing. Freezing denotes a temporary cessation of movement; scanning involves changes in head orientation.
A time budget measures how much of an observation interval is assigned to a behavioral category.

Treatments containing human-generated noise increased these behaviors during the playback period compared with relevant silent periods. The joint changes in movement, scanning and freezing provide a richer description of the response than retreat alone.
The reported behaviors were measured under the same playback timing, linking them to a controlled change in the environment.

Freezing could reduce self-generated ground noise, while scanning could alter available directional information. Those proposed functions were not isolated experimentally. The findings establish context-dependent behavior following seismic stimulation, not a demonstrated receptor channel, a brainstem computation or a uniquely seismic listening posture. Noise can be both a source of interference and a cue about possible environmental risk.
Human disturbance can change both received information and decisions about remaining at a site, and the experiment did not selectively separate those consequences.

items.text: Brain mass, regional volume and neuron number are different measurements; most counted elephant neurons are cerebellar.
Trigeminal trunk maps and facial motor subdivisions are specialized anatomical proposals, not complete functional circuit maps.
A trained Asian elephant detected 16 Hz at 65 dB SPL and localized brief broadband sources around one degree.
Foot Pacinian corpuscles and bone conduction supply anatomical and mechanical support, but their necessity for seismic behavior remains untested.
Ground-delivered alarm and noise stimuli change behavior; microphone controls are essential for excluding airborne leakage.
Different call and noise responses do not by themselves isolate caller recognition, threat meaning or a specific neural computation.
